latin: Beatitudo est essentialiter in actu intellectus.
translation: Beatitude is essentially in an act of the intellect.
translation_note: Edelheit quotes the printed thesis as 'Beatitudo est essentialiter in actu intellectus' (edelheit2022:10700). He also quotes its printed corollary, absent from Farmer's inventory line, as 'Correlarium: Nec fruitio, nec aliquis actus voluntatis, est essentialiter beatitudo' (edelheit2022:10700).
translator: original translation, drafted 2026-09-26 by WRITER-full-batch3, from Latin at farmer1998:11419
doctrine: The thesis makes beatitude (final human happiness) consist essentially in an act of intellect rather than of will, with a printed corollary denying that fruition or any act of will is essentially beatitude (edelheit2022:10700). Edelheit reads it as opening a series concerned with the relative powers of intellect and will in achieving beatitude (edelheit2022:10678). Farmer's note ties the thesis to the same intellect-versus-will axis that runs through the 'unity of intellect' series beginning at thesis 7.2, and states that Pico again represents Aquinas as an intellectualist at theses 2.19 and 2.28 (farmer1998:11497).
context: The thesis stands among a run of theses reported under Aquinas's name in the historical part of the 900 (section 2), the section through which Pico surveys positions before arguing his own view elsewhere in the work (farmer1998:11419).
historiography: Edelheit is the only scholar found discussing this thesis in the sources consulted; he treats it as the head of a short series on beatitude, intellect and will running through the following theses (edelheit2022:10678).

quotations.text: Thesis 12 leads us to considering the relation between beatitude, intellectual activity and the activity of the will.
Beatitudo est essentialiter in actu intellectus. Correlarium: Nec fruitio, nec aliquis actus voluntatis, est essentialiter beatitudo.
